overall_summary: Analysis of the deduplicated FACTVERSE performance data reveals a massive viewer preference for extreme space anomalies framed around interactive hypothetical scenarios ('What If You Fell Into...'). Videos focusing on bizarre planetary conditions, extreme weather on exoplanets, and high-value comparisons (e.g., diamond planets, burning ice) significantly outperform standard science or psychological facts in both views-per-day and like-to-view ratios. Content released within the last 7 days consistently commands higher velocity than older catalog entries, particularly space-oriented 'What If' hooks.

winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (IYuce8vaU3Y) pulled 1,024 views with 38 likes, and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (8KEl0_pJ_68) pulled 970 views with 18 likes within days.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on 'What If You Fell Into [Extreme Exoplanet]' formats using high-stakes spatial sensory hooks.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles featuring bizarre physical states like 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' (v1rrcZLdp4U) and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (QXuqYERlqSo) drove over 1,000 and 700 views respectively with strong engagement.
winning_patterns.action: Continue leveraging rare material conditions (gemstone weather, extreme darkness, absolute temperatures) paired with exclamation-driven curiosity hooks.

weak_patterns.pattern: Abstract Psychological Trivia without Sensory Stakes
weak_patterns.evidence: Shorts like 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (2fqaGqfsR4A) and 'Your Brain Is Hiding This From You' (mGEgENcGcNE) stagnated with single-digit or low double-digit views and zero engagement.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize flat psychological trivia unless anchored to an extreme physical anomaly or a visceral survival scenario.

weak_patterns.evidence: Videos such as 'The Only Animal That Can Live Forever' (F1kXwuXuNgo) and historical mysteries like 'The 2,000-Year-Old Mystery Science Can't Solve' (yLm-FjYH6-k) showed sluggish performance compared to space content.
weak_patterns.action: Shift animal and history concepts toward cinematic survival or high-conflict micro-narratives rather than standard educational trivia.

next_video.concept: What happens to your body if you step onto the metal-snow peaks of Kepler-13ab?
next_video.opening_direction: Start mid-action with the sound of roaring titanium winds and the visual of sparkling metallic snow rushing past the camera.
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the snow isn't water—it's vaporized titanium oxide freezing in the upper atmosphere and blanketing the dark side of the tidally locked world.
next_video.posting_window: 12:00 PM - 2:00 PM EST (Peak Space Content Engagement Window)
next_video.reason: Capitalizes on the proven high-performing 'What If' exoplanet format while introducing a brand-new celestial body (Kepler-13ab) and a fresh visual hook (titanium snow) to avoid repetition.
fresh_topic_constraints: Do not use diamond planets, burning ice, glass rain, or molten iron rain.
Must feature a newly introduced exoplanet (Kepler-13ab) with a distinct physical phenomenon.
Keep the script tightly paced under 21 seconds with a direct sensory payoff in the first 3 seconds.

experiment: Test a cinematic AI-generated visual of a human-scale object interacting with an extreme exoplanet material (titanium snow) in the first 2 seconds to measure if immediate visual novelty boosts 0-to-3-second retention compared to text-only title hooks.
